title: Effectiveness of a Generate→Validate→Repair Pipeline with Batfish for Intent-to-Configuration Translation: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We evaluate whether integrating a Batfish-style deterministic validator into a bounded generate→validate→repair pipeline reduces validator-detected deployment-risk configuration errors produced by an LLM intent-to-configuration translator. Following a sealed preregistration (CNSM2026-GenVal-Batfish-PR-v1) we ran a paired confirmatory study: 200 distinct intent-to-configuration tasks (four vendor/complexity strata, 50 per stratum), each with (A) LLM-only generation and (B) guarded generate→validate→repair (gpt-5-mini, ≤1 repair iteration). A deterministic Batfish-like validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) served as the harm oracle; primary estimand was the absolute paired difference in validator-clean rate (guarded − baseline). Results: both arms were validator-clean on all 200 tasks (baseline = 200/200, guarded = 200/200), yielding an estimate of 0.0 absolute difference (95% paired-bootstrap CI 0.0–0.0) and McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. The bounded repair loop was not invoked for any task because no initial validator-detected errors occurred. These confirmatory results show no measurable benefit for the guarded pipeline under the preregistered synthetic-task + sandboxed-validator conditions. We treat this as a defensible negative (null) confirmatory finding: in this setting the generator already satisfied the verifier. We report the preregistration, full execution manifest, raw outputs, and automated analysis artifacts, and discuss construct and external-validity limits (synthetic tasks, sandbox semantics, single model) and operational implications for where validator-in-the-loop controls add value.

sections.introduction: Large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent into low-level network configurations. While this promises efficiency gains, erroneous or unsafe configuration changes created by unconstrained generation can cause outages or security regressions. Prior work therefore advocates tooling around models—generate→validate→repair loops, sandboxing (e.g., Batfish), and human gates—to reduce deployment risk. We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment to test a focused operational claim: does adding a Batfish-style validator plus a bounded automatic repair iteration reduce validator-detected configuration errors compared to one-shot LLM generation? Our contributions: (1) a sealed preregistered paired design (n=200 tasks across four strata) with explicit estimand and analysis executor; (2) a full autonomous execution and analysis run using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic Batfish-like validator; (3) a transparent negative (null) confirmatory result with artifact-backed reconciliation and a discussion of why the guarded pipeline provided no measurable benefit in these conditions.
sections.related_work: Work on LLM-driven intent-to-configuration and NetOps automation documents both promise and risk: intent-based translation and in-context techniques have been proposed to generate configurations from natural language (e.g., Tu et al., 2024) while system and survey papers emphasize that operational reliability depends on the surrounding verification and orchestration machinery rather than model capability alone. Generate→validate→repair workflows and bounded self-correction are common mitigation proposals; other recent studies propose layered controls, RAG anchoring, and human-in-the-loop approval for safety. Contemporary platform and framework work (multi-agent orchestrators, tracing systems) further argue for workflow-centred evaluation rather than standalone model metrics. These prior findings motivated our preregistered confirmatory test using a deterministic validator as a concrete harm oracle.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: The study was preregistered as CNSM2026-GenVal-Batfish-PR-v1 (sealed plan; preregistration SHA-256 embedded in the execution manifest). Primary research question: Does a Batfish-based generate→validate→repair pipeline reduce validator-detected configuration errors versus LLM-only generation? Primary hypothesis H1: guarded yields a lower per-task validator-detected error rate. Secondary hypothesis H2: the bounded single-repair loop corrects >50% of initial errors. Sampling and tasks: 200 paired tasks (4 strata: IOS-like vs JunOS-like × single-step vs multi-step), 50 tasks per stratum. Inclusion/exclusion: synthetic public task corpus released with artifacts; tasks incompatible with sandbox features excluded before execution per preregistration (none excluded in the recorded run). Model and pipeline: model declared gpt-5-mini (provider: openai_responses), generation semantics: shared_initial_candidate; baseline = single model call producing final config; guarded = same initial generation plus deterministic validator run and at most one automated repair call if validator fails. Validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (Batfish-like scenario checks: reachability, ACL/policy, routing-loop and interface regressions) used as primary harm oracle. Analysis: paired binary outcome per task defined as 'validator-detected error' (1) vs 'validator-clean' (0) on final artifact; primary test McNemar two-sided (α=0.05); estimate absolute risk reduction with 10,000-resample paired bootstrap for 95% CI. Missingness policy: complete-pair primary; sensitivity analyses preregistered. All prompts, seeds, code, raw outputs and logs archived in the execution manifest.
sections.results: Execution and confirmatory analysis were completed per the sealed plan (planned episodes 400; completed 400; model calls used 200; no failed episodes). Summary contingency counts: baseline clean = 200, guarded clean = 200; discordant pairs n10 = 0, n01 = 0. Estimated absolute paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Paired-bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples; seed 1729). Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. Repair activity: zero tasks triggered a repair because no initial validator-detected errors were observed; repair_success_rate is undefined (no repairs invoked). All reported numbers and contingency tables match archived artifacts in the execution bundle (analysis/condition_summary.csv, paired_contingency_table.csv).
sections.discussion: Confirmatory interpretation: under the preregistered synthetic-task corpus and deterministic Batfish-like sandbox used here, the LLM-only generator produced validator-clean configurations for every task; consequently the guarded pipeline produced no observable improvement. This is a legitimate null result for the preregistered estimand: the generate→validate→repair intervention cannot reduce an error rate that is already zero on the chosen corpus and verifier. Exploratory diagnostics (from archived traces) suggest several nonexclusive explanations: (1) task difficulty and constrained templates in the synthetic corpus may have been within the generator's capability; (2) the shared-initial-generation strategy produced canonicalized outputs closely matching verifier expectations; (3) possibility of generator memorization or dataset-template alignment with model pretraining cannot be excluded and is treated as contamination risk per preregistration. Operational implication: validators remain necessary as a safety boundary, but their marginal benefit depends on task hardness, model capability, and sandbox fidelity; in low-difficulty/synthetic scenarios the pipeline's value may be limited. The null outcome also underscores the importance of matched, production-representative benchmarks when evaluating verifier-assisted agents.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory evaluation of a bounded generate→validate→repair pipeline using a Batfish-style deterministic validator and gpt-5-mini on 200 synthetic intent-to-configuration tasks. Both baseline and guarded arms were validator-clean on all tasks, producing an absolute paired difference of 0.0 (95% CI 0.0–0.0, McNemar p=1.0). This negative (null) confirmatory result demonstrates that, in this sandboxed synthetic setting, adding an automated single-repair iteration provided no measurable reduction in validator-detected errors because none occurred in the baseline. We release the preregistration, raw outputs, validator logs, and analysis artifacts. Future work should repeat analogous preregistered comparisons on production-representative, multi-vendor datasets, include adversarial and contamination-controlled tasks, and vary repair budgets and verifier expressiveness to locate regimes where verifier-in-the-loop pipelines yield quantifiable safety gains.

limitations: Confirmatory scope limited to a synthetic, public task corpus and deterministic Batfish-like sandbox; results do not generalize to production devices, heterogeneous vendor implementations, or richer harm oracles.
Single model tested (gpt-5-mini) and single bounded repair budget (≤1 repair). No cross-model claims are made.

Practical contamination risk: synthetic tasks may align with model pretraining or templated patterns (possible generator memorization); although contamination checks were recorded, this remains a construct-validity threat.
Repair loop was never invoked because baseline produced zero validator-detected errors; therefore secondary hypothesis about repair success (>50%) could not be evaluated.
Adversarial and prompt-injection scenarios were not included; security robustness under targeted attacks remains unresolved.
